title: Hopping coal trains and driving mules in 1917-18
summary: As the family gets poorer he hauls coal in the cold winter of 1917 and drives a mule team for $3.50 a day in the summer of 1918.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: As I grew a little older, things got a little rougher for the family and I would go out and seek jobs. And I can remember back in 1918 -- back in 1917 rather -- was a real cold winter. And most kids would -- young boy -- young kids would hop freight trains, jump up on the coal cars and throw off coal, and put that coal in a crocus sack and put it on our shoulders,
and haul that coal home so that we could have heat for the wintertime. That was in 1917.

I can remember in 1918 -- the summer of 1918 I got a job.-- it was during the war -- driving a team of mules. And back in those days they had what they called wheelers, a two wheel -- two wheels with a big shovel on it. And you had to get up early in the morning to go to the corral and put the collar and put the harness on your horse -- I mean on your mule. And I was too young to catch my mule, and the fellows would curse me out but they would help me put the harness on my mules.

And my salary during that time was three and a half a day, which was a lot of money. But I was trying to bring money into the family to help my father feed us all. And that job lasted through the summer. And, of course, later on in November of 1919, I think it was, was when the Armistice was signed.
